aspects.says: A parameter added so one shared method can serve both callers keeps each caller's rule in shared code, and a later change made without a flag, or in a branch both callers reach, still breaks the other caller.
basis: section:A Flag for Each Caller Keeps the Method Shared, and Every Change Must Be Checked Against Both

aspects.says: Inlining the method back, copying its body into each caller, substituting that caller's arguments and deleting what can no longer run, gives each owner code the other's change cannot reach.
basis: section:Inlining the Method Back Gives Each Format Its Own Code, and All Checks Pass

aspects.says: Code that looks alike but encodes two owners' rules, once merged, lets a change made for one caller break the other.
basis: section:Merging Look-Alike Code Ties Two Formats Together, and a Change for One Breaks the Other

aspects.says: The rule of three is a heuristic for when it is unclear whether copies must change together; one rule gets one home at the second copy, and look-alike copies of different rules stay apart at any count.
basis: section:The Rule of Three Is a Heuristic for When You Can't Yet Tell
